Keywords: error message, stack trace, traceback, exception, log, line number, first error
Description: Read the whole error, the full stack trace and the first error in the log before forming any theory.
When to Use: Any failure that produces a message, trace or non-zero exit code.
How to Apply: Find the first error (later ones are often consequences); note file:line, exception type and the values involved; open the code at that line.
Evidence: The exact message and the line it points to.
Pitfalls: Skimming to the last line; fixing a later error that is a consequence of the first.

Keywords: repro, reproduce, minimal example, isolate, steps to reproduce, test case
Description: Shrink the failing scenario until removing anything more makes the bug disappear.
When to Use: A bug you can trigger but not yet explain, or one buried in a large workflow.
How to Apply: Start from the failing case; remove inputs, steps and dependencies one at a time; keep each removal that still fails; turn the result into an automated test.
Evidence: A short script or test that fails reliably.
Pitfalls: Stopping while the repro still depends on unrelated setup.

Keywords: git log, recent commit, deploy, dependency bump, config change, what changed, regression, worked before
Description: If it used to work, the cause is usually in what changed: code, dependencies, config, data or infrastructure.
How to Apply: List commits, deploys, dependency updates and config changes since the last known-good state; compare lockfiles; read the diffs touching the failing path.
Evidence: The change list with the suspect change marked.
Pitfalls: Looking only at application code and missing dependency, config or data changes.

Keywords: git bisect, regression, find commit, good bad commit, binary search history
Description: Binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a regression.
When to Use: Behavior changed between two known commits and you have a reliable check.
How to Apply: git bisect start; git bisect bad <bad>; git bisect good <good>; run the check at each step or automate with git bisect run <script>.
Evidence: The first bad commit hash and its diff.
Pitfalls: A flaky check gives wrong verdicts; bisecting across commits that do not build.

Keywords: binary search, halve, bisect code, comment out, narrow down, isolate component
Description: Split the system in halves and check which half contains the fault, repeatedly.
When to Use: Large search spaces: long pipelines, big inputs, many components.
How to Apply: Check the data at a midpoint (log, assert, breakpoint); keep the half where it is already wrong; repeat until one unit remains.
Evidence: The smallest unit where correct input becomes wrong output.
Pitfalls: Changing code to test halves without reverting afterwards.

Keywords: hypothesis, scientific method, log, notes, theory, experiment, debugging journal
Description: Write each theory, the test that would kill it and the result, before and after running it.
When to Use: Any bug that is not solved within a few minutes.
How to Apply: For each hypothesis note: claim, prediction, test, observed result, verdict. Change one thing per test.
Evidence: The log table, ending in the confirmed root cause.
Pitfalls: Testing several theories at once; forgetting what was already ruled out.

Keywords: logging, trace, tracing, print debugging, observability, metrics, span, correlation id, debug log
Description: Add targeted logs or traces to see actual values and timing along the path.
When to Use: When you cannot attach a debugger or the bug only shows under real load or in production.
How to Apply: Log inputs, outputs and decisions at layer boundaries with an ID to correlate; use existing traces and metrics first; remove temporary logs afterwards.
Evidence: Log lines that show where the values diverge from expectation.
Pitfalls: Logging everything; leaving noisy or sensitive logs behind.

Keywords: compare, works here not there, diff environment, difference, working vs broken, staging vs production
Description: Compare a working case with a broken one and eliminate differences until the cause remains.
When to Use: It works in one place (environment, input, version, machine) and not another.
How to Apply: List every difference (versions, config, data, env vars, OS, timing); swap them one at a time toward the broken side until it breaks.
Evidence: The single difference that flips the result.
Pitfalls: Assuming two environments are identical without checking.

Keywords: flaky, repeat, loop, stress, race detector, shuffle, intermittent, concurrency, run many times
Description: Make a rare failure frequent by repeating the test under stress.
When to Use: Intermittent failures, races and order-dependent tests.
How to Apply: Run the test in a loop (for example 200 runs); shuffle test order; enable the race detector or sanitizers; limit CPU or add load; record the failure rate.
Evidence: The failure rate before and after the fix.
Pitfalls: Calling a fix done after a handful of green runs.

Keywords: profile, profiler, flame graph, cpu profile, heap profile, allocation, hotspot, pprof, py-spy, perf
Description: Measure where time and memory actually go.
When to Use: Any performance or memory problem, before changing code.
How to Apply: Profile the real workload (CPU, heap, allocations, I/O wait); read the flame graph top-down; confirm the hotspot with a micro-benchmark.
Evidence: Profile output naming the top contributors with percentages.
Pitfalls: Profiling a toy workload; optimizing what the profile does not show.

Keywords: data flow, call path, follow the data, callers, trace code, read code, who calls
Description: Follow a value from where it enters to where it is used, reading every function on the way.
When to Use: Understanding unfamiliar code, reviewing a change, or finding where data goes wrong.
How to Apply: Pick one concrete input; walk the call path through each function and branch; note transformations and side effects; check all callers of changed functions.
Evidence: The written call path with the step where behavior differs.
Pitfalls: Assuming what a function does from its name.

Keywords: rubber duck, explain, walk through, talk through, describe the code
Description: Explain the code line by line, out loud or in writing, as if to someone who knows nothing.
When to Use: Stuck on a bug or a design and going in circles.
How to Apply: State what each line should do and what it actually does; the gap usually appears in the explanation.
Evidence: The point where the explanation and the code disagree.
Pitfalls: Explaining what you think the code does instead of reading it.

Keywords: read tests, tests as documentation, examples, specification, usage, existing tests
Description: Read the existing tests to learn the intended behavior and how the code is meant to be called.
When to Use: Understanding unfamiliar code; before changing behavior; before adding tests.
How to Apply: Find the tests for the module (same name, test folders, grep for the function); read their setup and assertions; run them; use one as an entry point in a debugger.
Evidence: The tests that cover the code and what they assert.
Pitfalls: Trusting tests that are skipped, stale or assert nothing.
